L779@P18: extended to the west where horizontal street deposits show that the city wall wa~ originally
L780@P18: more than 3 m high and that it served as a revetment for houses at the top of the mound.
L781@P18: The city wall itself was over 6 m wide but in the later phases of the Period 3B occupation
L782@P18: the exterior was badly eroded and covered with debris thrown from the top of the mound.
L783@P18: It is these layers that have yielded the high quantity of inscribed pieces noted above.
L784@P18: In 1995, deep digging was continued in a small portion of Trench 11 through the stre'et
L785@P18: deposits that run along the exterior (eastern) face of the Mound E city wall. Approximately
L786@P18: 2.3 m of these deposits were found to underlie the latest preserved rebuilding of the city wall .
L787@P18: (possibly dating to the beginning of Period 3B), but the presence of some mud brick wash
L788@P18: layers suggest that there is an earlier city wall (possibly dating to Period 3A) offset to the
L789@P18: west. Below the Period 3 street deposits is debris dating to Period 2 (Early Harappan/
L790@P18: Harappan Transitional). This occupation is characterized by a .small mud brick house with
L791@P18: walls oriented north-south and east-west. Several cooking areas or hearths were discovered
L792@P18: along with pottery, beads and terracotta figurines.
L793@P18: One important find from the lowest levels is an inscribed chuck base mould for making
L794@P18: large jars (Fig. 12.9). The inscription is not simply graffiti, but was carefully and deeply
L795@P18: incised. Other moulds dating to Period 2 but with different .inscriptions have been found in
L796@P18: previous excavations in other areas of the site. This new discovery adds one more inscription
L797@P18: to the slo~ly increasing body of material that may demonstrate the emergence of writing at
L798@P18: the site. Additional important finds in these lowest levels are microbeads of fired paste,
L799@P18: possibly faience, and a bead made from steatite having a red slip and ~hite design. These
L800@P18: beads together with such items as copper chisels, terracotta cart wheels, and Black-on-red
L801@P18: painted pottery confirm that many of the characteristic features of the Harappan Phase
L802@P18: (Period 3) were already being produced during the Transitional Phase (Period 2).
L803@P18: The nlound of Period 2 is approximately 2 m high in the area beneath the Period 3 city
L804@P18: . wall as well as in the deep trench excavated in street .[95], 15 m to the east. These two deep
L805@P18: trenches show that the Period 2 mound rests on a natural surface that slopes gently to the
L806@P18: east and suggests that deposits of this phase extend for a considerable diste,tnce under Mound
L807@P18: ET.
L808@P18: Seals and Inscribed Objects
L809@P18: In the 1993, 1994, and 1995 seasons, about 130 inscribed small finds (not including
L810@P18: inscribed pottery) were recovered from the excavations on Mounds E and ET. Many of these
L811@P18: come fronl well documented trash and sometimes floor deposits witJ1 associated pottery and
L812@P18: small finds.. Some of the moulded faience and terracotta tablets were made from the same
L813@P18: moulds as pieces found in the earlier excavations on Mound AB and F (Vats, 1940). In
L814@P18: ~ddition, some of the incised steatite tablets have nearly identical inscriptions - only "nearly
L815@P18: identical" because .each has to be incised individually. Such a widespread distribution across
L816@P18: the site serves to suggest contemporaneity of occupation as well as socioeconomic and
L817@P18: perhaps ritual interaction between inhabitants of distinct sectors of the city (Kenoyer, 1995).
L818@P18: A number of these duplicate or nearly identical inscriptions are included in this report (Figs.
L819@P18: 7-11 and Table 2). In addifion a selection of new unique specimens is presented. Of special
L820@P18: note among these is the first inscribed piece of hard stone from Harappa - a fragment of
L821@P18: a vessel recovered from the surface of Mound AB (Fig. 12.3).

L916@P20: Joshi and Parpola (1987: H-220 to H-225). Unlike the incised copper tablets from Mohenjodaro, these tablets have raised script, Le., they are moulded in a fashion similar to- tablets
L917@P20: of faience and terracotta. So far, no incised copper tablets have been discovered from
L918@P20: Harappa and it appears that the two sites had very different traditions relating to the use of
L919@P20: tablets in general. At Harappa there are many more of the small moulded or incised tablets
L920@P20: of faience, terracotta, and steatite than there are at Mohenjo-daro. On the basis of our
L921@P20: excavations, we can begin to suggest that these tablets come from Periods 3B and 3C, with
L922@P20: the larger and more elaborate examples concentrated in 3C.

L1075@P23: stool to the proper left of the individual, on the "throne". The third scene depicts ~n
L1076@P23: .individual wearing a homed headress that has a triple projection in the centre. This human
L1077@P23: figure, perhaps a deity, also has bangles on the visible left arm. A fourth "scene" or motifgroup comprises six characters of script. Each of the six tablets thus depicts (or in the case
L1078@P23: of Fig. 9.4, depicted) two, three, or four parts of a story of text that appears to have been
L1079@P23: complete in four parts. Unknown, however, is whether the different combinations imply the
L1080@P23: same whole or whether they have different meanings or significations.
L1081@P23: All of these tablets appear to have been made from the same set of moulds. (The same
L1082@P23: has already been noted for the three larger tablets illustrated as Figs. 8.3 to 8.5.) It seems
L1083@P23: likely that' such pieces had a single locus of manufacture and point of distribution and then
L1084@P23: were carried to different parts of the site where they were subsequently incorporated into
L1085@P23: trash deposits. This pattern of distribution is also seen in other terracotta and faience tablets
L1086@P23: that were found in 1993 (Meadow and Kenoyer, 1994). A small tablet depicting a drummer
L1087@P23: (Fig. 9.7) is identical to one found on Mound AB (Vats, 1940, p. 146 and plate XCIII: 306)
L1088@P23: and a rhinoceros tablet from Harappa (not illustrated here) appears identical to ones found. iiL
L1089@P23: 1i at Mohenjo-daro (DK 5770 and VS 3513: Marshall, 1931).

L1093@P23: I'I: Mohenjo-daro is depicted here as Fig. 9.8. This mostly complete terracotta tablet is rectan11 gular in shape and has a plano-convex section. The flat side has a motif of a person spearing
L1094@P23: a male water buffalo. Above the hunting scene is a gharial and behind the hunter is a figure
L1095@P23: I wearing bangles and a homed and plumed headress and seated in the feet-together (yogic)
L1096@P23: position. On the opposite, convex, face is a figure grasping two felines (tiger and/or lion)
L1097@P23: and standing above an elephant. There is what appears to be a well-formed female breast
L1098@P23: depicted on this figure and a single Harappan sign is located above its head.
L1099@P23: The motif of a figure grasping two felines (usual~y tigers) by the neck is found on
L1100@P23: another tablet from Harappa (the twisted terracotta example illustrated in Fig. 9.6) and on
L1101@P23: tablets and seals from MOhenjo-daro. One of those from Mohenjo-daro !appears to depict a
L1102@P23: male with genitalia (Parpola, 1994, p. 247 and Franke-Vogt, 1991: Taffel XXXV: 248).
L1103@P23: Other examples are not so clear, but they have usually been assumed to represent males. As
L1104@P23: a likely female, the figure from Harappa conforms in sex with the depiction of a composite
L1105@P23: female-bovine figure grasping homed tiger' on a seal from Mohenjo-daro. (Franke-Vogt,
L1106@P23: 1991: Taffe1 XXXVI: 263). As Parpola (1994, p. 246) points out, the 'contest' motif is one
L1107@P23: of the most convincing and widely accepted parallels between Harappan and Near Eastern
L1108@P23: glyptic art." In the Harappan case, however, bulls and lions are replaced by tigers, and
L1109@P23: females as well as males are depicted as "hero(ine)". Another interesting feature of the
L1110@P23: tablets is that whereas the bovine especialiy are depicted as clearly male, the sex of the
L1111@P23: human figures is often not so evident.
L1112@P23: Part of the same contest motif as that in Fig. 9.8, apparently made from the same mould,
L1113@P23: is depicted on a broken terracotta tablet found by Vats east of the "working platforms" in
L1114@P23: the northeast comer of Trench IV, Mound F, some 4 to 7 feet below the surface. Conforming
L1115@P23: with the more complete example from our excavations, the convex side of the Vats tablet
L1116@P23: shows the lower half of the motif of a figure holding two felines and standing above an
L1117@P23: elephant (Vats, 1940, p. 59 plate XCIII: 308; Joshi and Parpola, 1987, p. 209: H-181).
L1118@P23: However, on the flat obverse of this broken tablet is a different scene, depicting a tiger
L1119@P23: looking back over its shoulder at an individual in a tree. ,This makes one more example of
